about: Golden vectors for the Invariant compiled-program IR. Any engine claiming to run this IR must produce these outputs, including the refusals. A refusal is part of the contract: an engine that rounds where this one rejects is not compatible.

vectors.name: move renames a field
vectors.why: The simplest op, and the one every other case is built on.

vectors.name: move into a nested object creates the parent
vectors.why: Unnesting and nesting are the same op, so the target may not exist.

vectors.name: move out of a nested object prunes the empty parent
vectors.why: Leaving `payment_method: {}` behind would not match the old contract.

vectors.name: move places a value beneath its own place
vectors.why: Meilisearch's list of a rule's actions became the pin list of an object in its place; the object is built where the list was.

vectors.name: move does nothing when the field is absent
vectors.why: An optional field a caller did not send must not appear as null.

vectors.name: scale moves the decimal point right
vectors.why: Multiplying by a hundred is wrong: 19.99 * 100 is 1998.9999999999998.

vectors.name: scale moves the decimal point left
vectors.why: The inverse has to be exact too, or a round trip loses money.

vectors.name: scale refuses a value it cannot represent exactly
vectors.why: Three decimal places scaled by two leaves a fraction of a minor unit. Rounding here would be silent data loss in money, so it refuses.

vectors.name: scale keeps a large integer exact
vectors.why: A value beyond double precision must not be rounded on the way through.

vectors.name: enum maps a known value
vectors.why: The ordinary vocabulary change.

vectors.name: enum refuses a value it has no mapping for
vectors.why: Passing an unmapped value through would hand the caller a word its contract never defined, and it would look like a success.

vectors.name: a lenient enum passes an unmapped value through
vectors.why: Only for a field naming another field, such as an error's `param`. An unfamiliar name there is harmless; failing the response is not.

vectors.name: set fills a field the caller omitted
vectors.why: A caller written before a required field existed never sends one.

vectors.name: set leaves a value the caller did supply
vectors.why: A default must never overwrite an explicit choice.

vectors.name: set writes a copy of its value at every place
vectors.why: An object written into every item is each item's own: a later write into one of them, as a restored action has its type put back, reaches that one alone.

vectors.name: del removes a field
vectors.why: The old contract never had it, so it must not be in the response.

vectors.name: set with ifNull fills a null and nothing else
vectors.why: A response field that became nullable is shown to an old caller with the value the provider chose, and never created where it was absent.

vectors.name: set with ifAbsent and ifNull fills either
vectors.why: A response field that became optional and nullable is always there, and never null, for an old caller.

vectors.name: del with ifNull drops a null and nothing else
vectors.why: A request field that no longer accepts null is left out when an old caller sends null, where the new contract lets it be absent.

vectors.name: del with ifNull leaves a value
vectors.why: Only the null the new contract refuses is dropped.

vectors.name: a wildcard applies to every element of a list
vectors.why: A list envelope is the common shape and the one with a fan-out cost.

vectors.name: a wildcard over an empty list does nothing
vectors.why: No elements is not an error, and must not be one.

vectors.name: a wildcard move creates the target in each element
vectors.why: Creating a slot per element is where a naive implementation goes wrong.

vectors.name: cast turns a number into a string
vectors.why: Some contracts carry identifiers as one and some as the other.

vectors.name: time writes epoch seconds as RFC 3339 in UTC
vectors.why: The commonest date change there is, and the output text is fixed: UTC, no fraction when it is zero.

vectors.name: time reads an offset as the instant it names
vectors.why: An offset is part of the text, not of the instant, so it moves the count and nothing else.

vectors.name: time keeps milliseconds as three digits
vectors.why: Whether the fraction is written, and how long it is, has to be the same in every engine.

vectors.name: time before 1970 and in the first century
vectors.why: Negative counts and years below 100 are where library date functions differ, so neither is used.

vectors.name: time refuses a fraction of a second going to whole seconds
vectors.why: Truncating would move the instant, and nobody asked for that.

vectors.name: time refuses a leap second
vectors.why: The epoch has no count for 23:59:60, and folding it into the next second is a guess.

vectors.name: time refuses a day that does not exist
vectors.why: A lenient parser rolls 29 February 2023 into March; this one refuses it.

vectors.name: time refuses a year RFC 3339 cannot write
vectors.why: Four digits of year is all the format has.

vectors.name: time leaves null alone
vectors.why: A nullable instant stays nullable in every format.

vectors.name: case rewrites each word
vectors.why: `in_progress` is `IN_PROGRESS` or `inProgress`, and every engine has to agree which.

vectors.name: case refuses words the target cannot keep apart
vectors.why: `a_1b` in camel case is `a1b`, which reads back as one word.

vectors.name: case refuses an acronym
vectors.why: `userID` could be `user_id` or `user_i_d`; neither is a guess to make for someone.

vectors.name: case refuses text not written in the case it names
vectors.why: A value that is not an identifier in the old convention is not one this op describes.

vectors.name: wrap puts each value in a list of one
vectors.why: A field that became a list, at every element of a list.

vectors.name: unwrap shows the one item
vectors.why: The inverse, for an old caller whose contract has the single value.

vectors.name: unwrap refuses a list of two
vectors.why: Showing the first would hide the second from a caller who cannot ask for it.

vectors.name: unwrap first shows the first of several, and leaves an empty list out
vectors.why: A provider may declare that one item stands for the list. Where there is none, the field is left out rather than shown as something it is not.

vectors.name: unwrap refuses an empty list
vectors.why: The old contract has a value there and cannot say there is none.

vectors.name: drop takes the values out of a list and keeps the rest in order
vectors.why: Asana stopped offering fields an old caller could ask for in opt_fields; the request goes on with everything else it asked for.

vectors.name: drop leaves an empty list where every value was dropped, and a list without them alone
vectors.why: The caller sent a list, so a list goes on; one with nothing to drop is not touched.

vectors.name: drop refuses a single value
vectors.why: A single value that is gone has no request left without it.

vectors.name: instructions apply in order
vectors.why: A rename followed by a conversion targets the new name. Applying them in any other order finds nothing and silently does half the work.

vectors.name: a wildcard at the cap transforms every element
vectors.why: The cap is a ceiling, not a sample: a body within it is transformed whole.

vectors.name: a wildcard past the cap at the end of a path is refused
vectors.why: Transforming the first N elements and leaving the rest is a body in the wrong shape that nothing reports. It is refused whole instead.

vectors.name: a wildcard past the cap in the middle of a path is refused
vectors.why: Dropping every match here would skip the instruction entirely, which is the same silent wrong shape. It is refused whole instead.

vectors.name: within runs a block at every element of a list
vectors.why: A Change to one element of a list is written once, relative to the element.

vectors.name: within reaches a value that is not an object, and an empty path rewrites it
vectors.why: A named vocabulary held where null is allowed too, as `anyOf: [Method, null]`, is reached by a within guarded on its type. Skipping a scalar there would leave every nullable use of the vocabulary unconverted while the plain uses are.

vectors.name: switch runs only the block for the variant the key names
vectors.why: A Change to one variant of a union must not touch the others, which may have a field of the same name meaning something else.

vectors.name: switch reads its key once, before the block can change it
vectors.why: Which variant a value is must not depend on what the block does to it.

vectors.name: switch on a number or a boolean matches its text
vectors.why: A discriminator is not always a string.

vectors.name: has runs its block only where the field is present
vectors.why: A union told apart by which field it has, rather than by a key's value.

vectors.name: has with absent runs its block only where a field is missing
vectors.why: Stripe's live and deleted objects share their type and differ only in that the deleted one carries `deleted`; the live one is known by its absence.

vectors.name: an object a within reached becomes its own id
vectors.why: A union gained a kind of object old callers never heard of. Stripe sends the id of an object a caller did not expand, and the old union allows it.

vectors.name: list items a within reached are removed, however many
vectors.why: Removing an item shifts the ones after it. Every one chosen has to go, and no other, whatever order they were found in.

vectors.name: a value a within reached is replaced with null
vectors.why: Where old callers could be sent null, a value they cannot read becomes one.

vectors.name: an instruction that would replace a whole body is refused
vectors.why: Only a value inside a body can be replaced; a body is what the caller sent.

vectors.name: a map wildcard reaches every value of an object
vectors.why: A price table keyed by currency, or metadata keyed by whatever the caller chose: the keys are data, and a Change reaches each value.

vectors.name: a move between maps keeps each value under its own key
vectors.why: Each map wildcard on the left lines up with one on the right, key by key.

vectors.name: a move from a list to a map is refused
vectors.why: A list index is not a key, so there is no telling where each value goes.

vectors.name: a map wildcard passes over a key that would reach a prototype
vectors.why: A body's keys are the caller's; one named __proto__ is never followed.

vectors.name: a key read through a wildcard is refused
vectors.why: A key is one value at one place; a wildcard would make it several.

vectors.name: blocks nested past the limit are refused
vectors.why: Each level multiplies how many places one instruction reaches.

vectors.name: a program naming a prototype key is refused
vectors.why: `__proto__` reaches an object every other object shares. A program is data from a build, and a build can be wrong; this must not be reachable.

vectors.name: call runs a named block where it stands
vectors.why: A block shared by every place a schema sits runs as if written at the call.

vectors.name: a block calls itself to follow a tree to its leaves
vectors.why: A schema that contains itself has no last place to list. The block descends and calls itself, so every level is translated, however deep.

vectors.name: is runs its block only where a value is of one kind
vectors.why: Stripe's expandable fields hold an id or the whole object. Only the object has fields to translate; the id passes untouched.

vectors.name: is tells a number however it was written
vectors.why: A number is a number whether or not it is kept as its exact digits.

vectors.name: a call to a block the contract does not have is refused
vectors.why: A program naming instructions it does not carry cannot be run as written.

vectors.name: blocks that call one another without descending are refused
vectors.why: A call runs where it stands, so a cycle that never moves into the value would never end. Only recursion that follows the value is allowed.

vectors.name: a contract calls the program's blocks, which call one another
vectors.why: A chain of contracts is linked, not written out: each contract's work ends in a call to the next contract's, held at the top of the program. An engine that only looked up a contract's own blocks could not run it.

vectors.name: a contract may not declare a block the program already does
vectors.why: One name meaning two things depending on who calls it is a program that runs differently on engines that resolve it differently.

envelopes.name: a query parameter is renamed
envelopes.why: The commonest parameter break, and the case every other one builds on.

envelopes.name: an untouched query parameter keeps its exact bytes and its place
envelopes.why: Re-encoding what no Change named would break a signature or a cache key that depends on those bytes, for no reason at all.

envelopes.name: a parameter the caller did not send stays unsent
envelopes.why: An optional parameter must not appear because a Change named it.

envelopes.name: a query number is scaled exactly
envelopes.why: Parameters are typed from their declaration, so a scale sees a number.

envelopes.name: a query value that is not a number is refused by the scale that needs one
envelopes.why: Text a number was declared for is passed to the instruction as text, which refuses it.

envelopes.name: a query value is mapped
envelopes.why: An enum rename on a parameter is the same instruction as on a field.

envelopes.name: a newly required query parameter is supplied
envelopes.why: A default an old caller never sent, added without overwriting one they did.

envelopes.name: a repeated query parameter becomes a comma-separated one
envelopes.why: The value is a list either way; only how the contract writes it changed.

envelopes.name: a header is renamed whatever case the caller wrote it in
envelopes.why: Header names are case-insensitive, so matching one exactly would miss it.

envelopes.name: a query parameter moves into a header
envelopes.why: Moving between locations is one move in one tree.

envelopes.name: a query parameter moves into the body
envelopes.why: A search that moves from the query string into a JSON body is a location move like any other, and the body is read only because a program reaches it.

envelopes.name: a path parameter is mapped and written back into the path
envelopes.why: A path parameter can be converted in place; the template is unchanged.

envelopes.name: a path parameter can only be converted
envelopes.why: A template has the parameters it has, so moving one out is refused at load.

envelopes.name: a cookie is renamed and the others are kept
envelopes.why: Cookies are addressed one by one; the rest of the header is not the program's.

envelopes.name: a deepObject is renamed, and a prototype key in it is dropped
envelopes.why: Property names in a deepObject are the caller's to choose, `__proto__` included, and it must never become a key of anything.

envelopes.name: a header value that would break the line is refused
envelopes.why: A line break in a header value is how a request is smuggled.

envelopes.name: a program touching a credential header is refused
envelopes.why: A program that can move a credential can move it somewhere it is logged.

envelopes.name: a program naming a parameter it does not declare is refused
envelopes.why: Every parameter a program rewrites has to say how it is written.

envelopes.name: a program addressing every query parameter at once is refused
envelopes.why: A wildcard over the query string would rewrite parameters nobody declared.

envelopes.name: a query parameter moves into a form body, beside changes inside it
envelopes.why: Stripe takes form bodies, and a parameter that moves into one has to be written the way the form writes it, with every pair nobody named kept.

envelopes.name: a query parameter is renamed beside a change inside an XML body
envelopes.why: CloudSearch's DefineIndexField takes its version in the query and its field in an XML body, and a release changed both at once.

envelopes.name: a query parameter moves into an XML body under the name its contract gives it
envelopes.why: A value that moves into an XML body is written as the element the current contract describes, after everything the caller wrote.

forms.name: a nested field is renamed in bracketed keys
forms.why: Stripe writes nested fields as `metadata[order]=`, and a rename inside one is the commonest nested change.

forms.name: a pair no instruction names keeps its exact bytes
forms.why: Re-encoding what no Change named would change bytes someone may depend on, for no reason.

forms.name: a field in every element of a list is renamed
forms.why: Stripe writes lists of objects as `items[0][price]=`, and the wildcard has to reach each one.

forms.name: a repeated plain field is renamed and stays repeated
forms.why: Twilio writes a list as the same key repeated, with no brackets.

forms.name: a plain field's value is mapped
forms.why: An enum rename is the same instruction in a form as in JSON.

forms.name: a newly required field is supplied
forms.why: A default an old caller never sent, without overwriting one they did.

forms.name: a null is written as an empty value
forms.why: An empty value is how a form says unset, which is what Stripe reads it as.

forms.name: a prototype key inside a bracketed field is dropped
forms.why: Keys inside brackets are the caller's to choose, and `__proto__` must never become one.

forms.name: a value a number was declared for, written as text, is refused by the scale
forms.why: The form carries text; typing it is what lets a scale refuse what is not a number.

forms.name: a declaration naming a prototype key is refused
forms.why: A program is data from a build, and a build can be wrong.

statuses.name: a status is answered as the one the old contract promised, without a body it never promised
statuses.why: Gitea 1.25 answers 201 with the variable it created where 1.24 answered 204 with nothing; an old caller checks for 204.

statuses.name: a status promised with no body is answered with an empty one of length zero
statuses.why: Immich 1.138 answers 204 where 1.137 answered 200 with nothing, and a 200 says how long its body is.

statuses.name: a body both statuses carry is served as any body is, with the work for the provider's status
statuses.why: The rest of the release's Changes are filed under the status the provider answers with, which is the one an engine reads.

statuses.name: rules apply in turn, each to the status the one before answered
statuses.why: A chain of releases is one list: the later release's rule first, then the earlier one's, as a response undoes the later release first.

statuses.name: a status no rule names is answered as it came
statuses.why: A rule is about one status; every other answer of the operation is the provider's.

statuses.name: a rule that would send a body with a 204 is refused
statuses.why: A 204 never carries a body, so a program that says otherwise was not compiled by anyone who read it.

statuses.name: a rule that answers a status as itself is refused
statuses.why: It says nothing, and a program that says nothing where it claims to is refused rather than trusted.

statuses.name: a rule that answers with a status that is not a success is refused
statuses.why: Only a success status an old caller was promised is ever answered in place of another.

xml.name: a document nothing changes comes out byte for byte
xml.why: Re-encoding what no Change touched would change bytes someone may depend on: the declaration, comments, quotes, references and indentation all stay.

xml.name: a value is mapped in place
xml.why: An enum rename is the same instruction in XML as in JSON, and only the element's text changes.

xml.name: a value in every item of a wrapped list is mapped
xml.why: CloudFront lists distributions inside an <Items> wrapper, each item named for its type, and a vocabulary change reaches each one.

xml.name: items of a list written in place keep their places among other elements
xml.why: An unwrapped list's items are siblings of other fields, and each is written back where it stood.

xml.name: a field a new contract requires is supplied before the end tag's indent
xml.why: A default an old caller never sent, written where the document's own layout puts a last child.

xml.name: a default is not written over a value the caller sent
xml.why: `ifAbsent` is the same promise in XML: what the caller wrote stays.

xml.name: a field is written into an element that was empty
xml.why: `<Config/>` has no end tag to write before, so it gains one.

xml.name: an object is written with the names its contract gives it
xml.why: A default that is an object is written as elements, each named as the contract names it.

xml.name: a field an old contract does not have is removed with what it holds
xml.why: Removing a field removes its element, whatever is inside it; the indentation around it stays.

xml.name: a renamed field is written under its new name, attributes and contents as they came
xml.why: A rename is the commonest change there is; an element's attributes and every child nothing names travel with it untouched.

xml.name: a value moved into an object that was not there is written inside it
xml.why: A field that moved beneath a new parent creates the parent, named as the contract names it.

xml.name: an attribute's value is mapped
xml.why: A field the contract writes as an attribute is read and written as one.

xml.name: a new attribute is added to the start tag
xml.why: A default the contract writes as an attribute goes where attributes go.

xml.name: a number written as text is scaled exactly
xml.why: A value the contract types as a number reaches the instruction as one, digits and all.

xml.name: a new element takes the default namespace it is written in
xml.why: Amazon writes every element in the namespace its root declares; a field the program adds is in it too, without a declaration of its own.

xml.name: a new element in a declared namespace uses the prefix bound to it
xml.why: A description with a prefix and a namespace writes the prefix, declaring it only where it is not already bound.

xml.name: an element matches its description only in the namespace it names
xml.why: Two elements with one local name in different namespaces are different fields; the one in another namespace is kept as it came.

xml.name: an element moved out of a namespace's scope keeps its namespace
xml.why: Moving an element from under a declaration to where the prefix is not bound would change what its contents mean, so the declaration goes with it.

xml.name: text a program writes is escaped
xml.why: A value holding markup characters must stay a value, never become markup.

xml.name: references are read as the characters they stand for
xml.why: `A` and `&` are the text `A&`, which is what a map compares.

xml.name: a value an instruction leaves as it was keeps how it was written
xml.why: A map that sends a value to itself changes nothing, so the reference it was written with stays.

xml.name: a line break is read as XML reads one
xml.why: A carriage return and line feed in text is one line feed to an XML reader, whatever the bytes.

xml.name: a CDATA section is read as its text
xml.why: CDATA is text written without escaping, and means the same as the escaped text.

xml.name: a byte order mark stays where it was
xml.why: Some servers write one; it is not part of the root element.

xml.name: a value becomes a list of one written in place
xml.why: `wrap` makes a list, and a list written in place is its item repeated under the list's item name.

xml.name: a list of one becomes its item
xml.why: `unwrap` stands the item where the list's first item stood.

xml.name: values the new contract refuses are taken out of a wrapped list
xml.why: `drop` removes items and leaves the others, and the wrapper's layout, as they were.

xml.name: an item a list gains follows its last item
xml.why: A list written in place that grew keeps its items where they were and writes the new ones after the last.

xml.name: a place the writing description does not name keeps the names it had
xml.why: Only what a description names is renamed; a list read and left where it was keeps its items' names, found by the round-trip property.

xml.name: a place no instruction reads is moved whole, whatever it holds
xml.why: A field whose contract says nothing of what it holds is moved as it came, text, elements and attributes alike, under its new name.

xml.name: an attribute the old contract does not have is taken off the start tag
xml.why: Removing a field written as an attribute removes the attribute and leaves the element's other attributes as they came.

xml.name: an attribute a program writes is escaped
xml.why: Quotes, markup characters and line breaks in an attribute's value must stay its value, and a line break must survive being read again.

xml.name: a wrapped list that held nothing gains its items inside its wrapper
xml.why: The wrapper stays where it was and keeps its layout; the items go before the indent of its end tag.

xml.name: a list written in place becomes a wrapped one under a new name
xml.why: A contract that started wrapping a list writes the wrapper its description names around the items.

xml.name: a renamed wrapped list keeps its layout, its items renamed with it
xml.why: The wrapper and each item are written under the names the new description gives them, and everything between them stays.

xml.name: a number is written back with the digits it has
xml.why: Scaling down writes the exact decimal, never a rounded double.

xml.name: a document type declaration is refused
xml.why: Entities are how XML bombs and external fetches get in; with no declaration there are none, so one is refused outright.

xml.name: an external entity is refused
xml.why: A document that names a file or a URL to read in must never make the runtime read it.

xml.name: a reference to an entity XML does not define is refused
xml.why: Without a declaration, ` ` names nothing, and guessing what it meant is not reading XML.

xml.name: text among an object's elements is refused
xml.why: Mixed content has no place in a tree of fields, and dropping it would lose it.

xml.name: attributes on a value the contract describes as text are refused
xml.why: A value is written back as text, and attributes nothing describes would be lost on the way.

xml.name: an encoding other than UTF-8 is refused
xml.why: The body was read as UTF-8, so one that says otherwise was not read as it was written.

xml.name: an attribute written twice is refused
xml.why: Well-formed XML names each attribute once, and which one to believe is a guess.

xml.name: a prefix nothing declares is refused
xml.why: An element's namespace is part of its name, and an undeclared prefix leaves it unknown.

xml.name: an end tag that does not match is refused
xml.why: A document that is not well-formed is not XML.

xml.name: content after the root element is refused
xml.why: A document has one root; a second is a second document.

xml.name: a field written twice where the contract has one is refused
xml.why: Which of the two an instruction should read is a guess.

xml.name: a character XML does not allow is refused
xml.why: A control character cannot appear in XML, even written as a reference.

xml.name: a body nested past the limit is refused as too large
xml.why: Every step follows the nesting, and a body of a hundred thousand open tags must not exhaust the stack.

xml.name: a document of more namespace declarations than any real one is refused
xml.why: Each element that declares a namespace copies the ones in scope, so thousands of declarations under deep nesting would cost their product.

xml.name: a null is refused by the change that wrote it
xml.why: XML has no null, and writing nothing or an empty element would be a guess about what the caller means.

xml.name: a description of a list of lists is refused
xml.why: OpenAPI gives a list of lists no XML form, so there is nothing to read it as.

xml.name: a description that writes two fields as one element is refused
xml.why: An element that could be either field is a guess about which.

xml.name: a program that reads a map's values in an XML body is refused
xml.why: XML has no maps, and a map's wildcard would reach the elements nothing names.
